Title: Failure To Restrict URL Access
Result: It was observed that the application's video streaming URL can be directly accessed and the video file can be downloaded without adequate access restrictions.
Description: Applications are not always protecting page requests properly. Sometimes, URL protection is managed via configuration, and the system is misconfigured. Also code level protection can be used.
Solution:
Access control checks must be performed before a request to a sensitive function is granted, which ensures that the user is authorized to access that function.
Implement server-side authorization checks before serving video content.
Ensure only authenticated and authorized users can access each video.
Do not rely solely on the video URL or object ID for access control.
Use short-lived, signed URLs or access tokens for protected video resources.
Validate that the requesting user has permission to access the requested video.
Prevent direct access to video resources when the user is not authorized.

Title: Directory Traversal
Result: It was observed that the application accepts an encoded path traversal sequence and resolves the request to an unintended /api/users endpoint.
Description: Path traversal exploits insufficient security validation in web applications and aims to access the files from a restricted path of the system by navigating the file system of the server. This attack is also known as a "dot dot slash" attack or directory traversal attack.
Solution:
Strict access control should be implemented in the web application in order to restrict access to system files.

Properly normalize and canonicalize URL paths before processing requests. Reject encoded and unencoded traversal sequences such as ../ and ..%2f where they are not required. Implement strict allowlisting for valid API endpoints. Apply authorization checks to the final resolved endpoint. Configure the web server, reverse proxy, and application framework to consistently handle encoded path separators and traversal sequences. Test the application against encoded, double-encoded, and alternate path normalization techniques.

Title: Encryption Decryption Attack
Result: It was observed that the application exposes the encryption secret in the client-side JavaScript bundle, allowing an attacker to decrypt captured encrypted requests/responses and generate modified encrypted requests.
Description:
Encryption is a crucial security measure used to protect sensitive information by converting it into an unreadable format, which can only be reverted to its original form using a specific key and initialization vector (IV). When these cryptographic keys are improperly managed, such as being hardcoded into the application or configuration files, they become vulnerable to exposure and misuse.

Risk
• Data Exposure: The hardcoded private key and exposed decryption logic enable unauthorized access to sensitive data, leading to potential data breaches.
• Security Compromise: Attackers exploiting these vulnerabilities can decrypt and access protected information, compromising the confidentiality of user data.
• Underlying Vulnerability Exploitation: Successful decryption facilitates the exploitation of additional vulnerabilities discovered, intensifying the impact of the attack.
• Reputation Damage: Data breaches and security compromises harm the organization's reputation, eroding trust among users and stakeholders.
Solution:
Never hardcode cryptographic keys or IVs in the source code or configuration files.
IVs should be unique and unpredictable for each encryption operation. Typically, this can be achieved by using a secure random number generator.
IVs can be stored alongside the ciphertext, as they do not need to be kept secret but should never be reused with the same key.
Do not embed encryption keys, secrets, or other sensitive cryptographic material in client-side JavaScript.
Perform encryption and decryption of sensitive application data on the server side using securely stored server-side keys.
Store cryptographic keys in a secure key-management system or secrets manager rather than source code or frontend bundles.
Implement proper server-side authentication and authorization for every sensitive API operation.
Do not rely on client-side encryption as a security boundary.
Rotate the exposed encryption key immediately and invalidate any previously generated encrypted tokens/data where applicable.
Review application logs and source code for other exposed secrets or hardcoded credentials.
Note: Implement the provided mitigation through the application and ensure the encryption key is no longer accessible to unauthorized clients.

Title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
Result: It was observed that the application allows a malicious SVG file containing JavaScript to be uploaded and stored, resulting in JavaScript execution when the uploaded file is accessed.
Description:
The Web application is vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS), which allows attackers to take advantage of Web server scripts to inject JavaScript or HTML code that is executed on the client-side browser. This vulnerability is often caused by server-side scripts written in languages such as PHP, ASP, .NET, Perl or Java, which do not adequately filter data sent along with page requests or by vulnerable HTTP servers. This malicious code appears to come from your Web application when it runs in the browser of an unsuspecting user. An attacker can do the following damage with an exploit script:
  • access other sites inside another client's private intranet
  • steal another client's cookie(s)
  • modify another client's cookie(s)
  • steal another client's submitted form data
  • modify another client's submitted form data before it reaches the server
  • submit a form to your Web application on the user's behalf that modifies passwords or other application data
The two most common methods of attack are:
  • Having a user click a URL link sent in an e-mail
  • Having a user click a URL link while visiting a Web site
In both scenarios, the URL will generally link to the trusted site, but will contain additional data that is used to trigger the XSS attack. Note that SSL connectivity does not protect against this issue. Stored Cross-Site Scripting occurs when an application stores user-controlled content and later renders it in a web browser without properly sanitizing or encoding it. In this case, an SVG file containing a JavaScript payload was uploaded through the file upload functionality. The uploaded SVG was accessible through the application and rendered by the browser, causing the embedded JavaScript to execute.
Solution:
Fix Cross Site Scripting Vulnerability Restrict uploads to required image formats and block SVG files if they are not required. Validate the file extension, MIME type, and actual file content server-side. Sanitize SVG files and remove scripts, event handlers, embedded HTML, and other active content. Store uploaded files outside the application's executable/web content directory. Serve uploaded files with safe Content-Type and Content-Disposition headers. Consider serving uploaded files from a separate domain/origin. Implement a restrictive Content Security Policy as an additional security control. Audit the affected url and other similar dynamic pages or scripts that could be relaying untrusted malicious data from the user input. In general, the following practices should be followed while developing dynamic web content:
  • Explicitly set the character set encoding for each page generated by the web server
  • Identify special characters
  • Encode dynamic output elements
  • Filter specific characters in dynamic elements
  • Examine cookies
For more information on the above practices, read the following CERT advisory: CERT Advisory CA-2000-02
  • For ASP.NET applications, the validateRequest attribute can be added to the page or the web.config. For example: 
            <%@ Page ... validateRequest="true" %>

        OR
    In addition, all dynamic content should be HTML encoded using HTTPUtility.HTMLEncode.
  • For PHP applications, input data should be validated using functions such as strip_tags and utf8_decode. Dynamic content should be HTML encoded using HTML entities.
  • For Perl applications, input data should be validated whenever possible using regular expressions. Dynamic content should be HTML encoded using HTML::Entities::encode or Apache::Util::html_encode (when using mod_perl).

Title: File Upload Vulnerability(Unrestricted File Upload)
Result: It was observed that the application allows uploading files with an executable .exe extension through the video upload functionality without enforcing a proper file type restriction.
Description:
Unrestricted file upload occurs when an application accepts files without properly validating their extension, MIME type, and actual file content. In the observed case, the video upload functionality accepted a file named with an .exe extension while the request declared its content type as video/mp4. The server processed the upload successfully and stored the file, indicating insufficient server-side validation of the uploaded file type.

The application allows users to upload files without properly validating the file type or extension. While no code execution is confirmed, the ability to upload potentially dangerous files (e.g., .php, .jsp) increases the risk of server-side compromise if further misconfigurations exist.

This can lead to Remote Code Execution (RCE), data exfiltration, or website defacement, especially if the uploaded files are accessible via a public directory.
Solution:
Allow only required video extensions such as .mp4, .webm, and other approved formats.

Validate the file extension, MIME type, and actual file signature/content on the server side.

Do not rely on the Content-Type header or client-side validation.

Reject executable extensions such as .exe, .bat, .cmd, .sh, .dll, .php, .jsp, and similar potentially dangerous file types.

Store uploaded files outside the web root where possible.

Rename uploaded files using server-generated random names and avoid preserving user-controlled extensions.

Configure the file storage location so uploaded content cannot be executed as server-side code.

Implement file size limits and malware/antivirus scanning where appropriate.

Implement Strict Allowlist Validation
Only allow specific, safe file types (e.g., .jpg, .png, .pdf) and validate both the extension and MIME type on the server side.

Store Files Outside the Web Root
Prevent direct access to uploaded files by storing them in directories not served by the web server.

Rename Uploaded Files and Sanitize Input
Use random or hashed filenames (e.g., UUIDs) and remove any user-supplied extensions to prevent execution.

Title: Missing Web API Rate Limiting
Result: It was observed that the file upload API does not enforce adequate rate limiting, allowing multiple upload requests to be submitted within a short period.
Description: Web API (Application Programming Interfaces)  is a framework which allows you to build HTTP services for Web Servers or Web Clients. Web API rate limiting is defined to control the rate of requests that an user can make to a Web API in a given span of time. Attacker can perform DDOS attacks by sending massive amount of API requests if rate limiting or throttling is missing and can misuse the API service.
Solution:
It is recommended to implement Throttling / rate-limit in either ways - /n 1. user / IP based rate-limit: this defines the number of request a user or a client IP can make per the span of time. /n 2. Server based: this defines the server rejecting the requests post a threshold is reached for handling the requests; not restricting to any specific user.
In either case; this will allow legit traffic and requests to be processed by the server and avoid redundant data.
Limit the number of upload requests per user/IP within a defined time window.
Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests when the limit is exceeded.
Apply limits based on authenticated user identity as well as source IP.
Enforce reasonable file-size and total-storage quotas.
Implement monitoring and alerting for unusually high upload activity.
Consider temporary blocking or progressive delays for repeated violations.

Solution:
Recommendation: Implement a strict CSP policy with at least the following: "default-src 'self'"; "script-src 'self' 'nonce-random'"; "object-src 'none'"; "base-uri 'none'"; "frame-ancestors 'none'"; "style-src 'self'"; "img-src 'self'"; "connect-src 'self'"; "form-action 'self'".
Remove unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval where they are not required.
Use CSP nonces or hashes for required inline scripts.
Remove unnecessary localhost/development endpoints from the production CSP.
Use HTTPS for permitted external resources.
Restrict connect-src to only trusted and required production endpoints.

Title: Overly Broad Cookie Path Detected
Result: It was observed that the session authentication cookie was configured with the root path (/), allowing it to be sent with requests to all application paths.
Description: The cookie 'path' attribute signifies the URL or path for which the cookie is valid. Exposing the cookie to all web applications on the domain can lead to sensitive information disclosure like session identifier, etc. and can cause one application to compromise another application.
Solution:
It is suggested that 'path' cookie attributes must be properly set in an environment where subdomains and subfolders host different applications.
Configure the authentication/session cookie with the narrowest possible Path value required by the application instead of /. For example, if the cookie is only required under /login or a specific application path, restrict it accordingly. Continue using Secure, HttpOnly, and an appropriate SameSite attribute.

Title: Sensitive HTML Form Fields With auto-complete Enabled
Result: It was observed that the password field has autocomplete enabled, which may allow browsers to store and automatically populate sensitive authentication information.
Description:
The Web form contains passwords or other sensitive text fields for which the browser auto-complete feature is enabled. 
   Auto-complete stores completed form field and passwords locally in the browser, so that these fields are filled 
   automatically when the user visits the site again.
	
   
Sensitive data and passwords can be stolen if the user's system is compromised.
	
   
Note, however, that form auto-complete is a non-standard, browser-side feature that each browser handles differently. 
   Opera, for example, disregards the feature, requiring the user to enter credentials for each Web site visit.
Solution:
Disable autocomplete for all sensitive fields. For each sensitive field in the HTML, set the "autocomplete" attribute to "off". For example:
If there are many fields, it may be faster to set the "autocomplete" attribute to "off" in the outer
tag. For example:
Review whether password autocomplete is required for the application's security requirements. For sensitive authentication scenarios where browser storage is not desired, configure the password field appropriately to discourage credential retention. Avoid storing passwords in application-side storage, cookies, or client-side JavaScript. Apply appropriate endpoint and browser security controls, particularly on shared or sensitive systems.
